sources.title: NCBI Bookshelf: Principles of Wound Healing

questions.question: A long-term smoker has replacement of normal ciliated columnar bronchial epithelium by stratified squamous epithelium. Which consequence best captures why this adaptation is clinically important?
choices: The new epithelium tolerates irritation better but reduces mucociliary defense and may progress toward dysplasia
The change increases ciliary clearance and eliminates cancer risk
The change is hyperplasia of normal ciliated cells and is always irreversible
The change represents acute necrosis with immediate airway perforation
rationales: Squamous metaplasia improves resistance to chronic irritation but sacrifices cilia and mucus clearance; persistent injury can favor dysplastic change.
Squamous epithelium lacks the normal ciliary function and does not eliminate malignancy risk.
Metaplasia is replacement by a different mature cell type and may regress if the stimulus is removed.
Viable metaplastic tissue is not synonymous with acute necrosis.
questions.explanation: A useful clinical interpretation weighs the short-term protective adaptation against impaired function and longer-term neoplastic risk.

questions.question: A 38-year-old with chronic anovulation has prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure and abnormal uterine bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows increased gland number without invasion. Which adaptation is most likely?
choices: Pathologic hyperplasia caused by persistent hormonal stimulation
Hypertrophy caused only by increased individual gland-cell size
Metaplasia caused by replacement with squamous epithelium
Atrophy caused by loss of estrogen signaling
rationales: Hormonal stimulation can drive an increase in endometrial cell number, producing hyperplasia and possible progression to atypia.
The defining change is increased cell number rather than only increased size.
The stem does not describe replacement by another mature cell phenotype.
Unopposed estrogen stimulates rather than suppresses endometrial growth.
questions.explanation: Pathologic hyperplasia is controlled growth in response to stimulation, but persistent stimulation can increase malignant potential and requires appropriate evaluation.

questions.question: An older adult loses substantial quadriceps mass after six weeks of bed rest. Which intervention most directly targets the dominant adaptation?
choices: Progressive mobilization and resistance activity as clinically safe to reverse disuse atrophy
Long-term immobilization to allow cardiomyocyte hyperplasia
Antibiotics to suppress neutrophil-mediated muscle necrosis
High-dose glucocorticoids to stimulate muscle protein synthesis
rationales: Reduced workload promotes protein loss and smaller myofibers; graded loading can help reverse disuse atrophy when safe.
Immobilization worsens disuse atrophy, and cardiomyocytes are not the affected tissue.
The case describes disuse, not bacterial myonecrosis.
Glucocorticoid excess can promote muscle catabolism rather than restore mass.
questions.explanation: The cause of atrophy matters. Correcting disuse requires restoring safe mechanical and functional demand while addressing nutrition and comorbidity.

questions.question: Minutes after an insect sting, a patient develops a raised, erythematous wheal at the site. Which microvascular event most directly produces the swelling?
choices: Histamine-mediated endothelial gap formation with protein-rich fluid leaving postcapillary venules
Arteriolar constriction that lowers local hydrostatic pressure
Immediate collagen deposition by fibroblasts
Decreased vascular permeability with intravascular protein retention
rationales: Histamine increases permeability in postcapillary venules, allowing protein-rich exudate and water to enter tissue.
Vasodilation, not sustained constriction, contributes to redness and warmth.
Collagen deposition occurs later during repair and does not explain an immediate wheal.
Decreased permeability would oppose edema formation.
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation combines vascular dilation with increased permeability, explaining redness, warmth, and localized edema.

questions.question: A previously healthy patient with bacterial cellulitis improves after therapy. Which change in the inflammatory infiltrate is expected as the process moves from early acute inflammation toward cleanup and repair?
choices: Neutrophil predominance gives way to monocytes and macrophages that remove debris and coordinate repair
Eosinophils permanently replace all phagocytes
Platelets become the principal antigen-presenting cells
Fibroblasts disappear before extracellular matrix remodeling begins
rationales: Neutrophils dominate many early bacterial responses; recruited monocytes become macrophages that clear debris and signal repair.
Eosinophils are prominent in selected parasitic and allergic responses, not universal resolution.
Platelets support hemostasis and signaling but are not the principal antigen-presenting cells in this sequence.
Fibroblasts become important in matrix production and remodeling rather than disappearing.
questions.explanation: Inflammation and repair overlap. A change in cellular participants reflects transition from pathogen control toward debris clearance and tissue reconstruction.

questions.question: A patient has chronic cough, weight loss, and upper-lobe cavitary disease. Biopsy shows macrophages transformed into epithelioid cells surrounded by lymphocytes. What does this pattern represent?
choices: Granulomatous inflammation attempting to contain a persistent stimulus
A purely neutrophilic response to a rapidly cleared stimulus
Immediate type I hypersensitivity without cellular recruitment
Normal regenerative hyperplasia with no inflammatory significance
rationales: Granulomas organize activated macrophages and lymphocytes around a difficult-to-eradicate agent or material.
A transient neutrophilic response does not produce the described epithelioid granuloma.
Immediate hypersensitivity is mast-cell mediated and does not explain this chronic histology.
The organized inflammatory pattern is pathologic, not normal regeneration.
questions.explanation: Granulomatous inflammation narrows the differential but is not itself an organism-specific diagnosis; microbiologic and clinical correlation remain necessary.

questions.question: An older adult with fever and suspected infection has a markedly elevated C-reactive protein. Which signaling pathway most directly explains hepatic production of this acute-phase reactant?
choices: Proinflammatory cytokine signaling, especially interleukin-6, stimulates hepatocytes
Histamine directly converts albumin into C-reactive protein
Complement C9 enters hepatocyte nuclei and activates coagulation
Erythropoietin suppresses hepatic protein synthesis
rationales: IL-6 and other inflammatory cytokines stimulate hepatic acute-phase protein synthesis.
CRP is newly synthesized; it is not converted from albumin by histamine.
C9 participates in the membrane attack complex and does not serve this nuclear signaling role.
Erythropoietin primarily supports erythroid production and does not explain an elevated CRP.
questions.explanation: CRP is a nonspecific marker of inflammatory signaling. Trends can help evaluate trajectory but cannot establish a diagnosis by themselves.

questions.question: A febrile patient asks why an NSAID can lower temperature without eliminating the infectious trigger. Which explanation is most accurate?
choices: Cyclooxygenase inhibition reduces prostaglandin-mediated elevation of the hypothalamic temperature set point
The medication immediately destroys circulating microbial DNA
The medication blocks all cytokine production permanently
The medication causes neutrophils to undergo uncontrolled necrosis
rationales: Pyrogenic signaling increases hypothalamic prostaglandin E2; cyclooxygenase inhibition reduces this set-point signal.
Antipyretic action is not direct antimicrobial killing.
NSAIDs do not permanently eliminate all cytokine production.
Neutrophil necrosis is not the therapeutic mechanism of fever reduction.
questions.explanation: Symptom control and treatment of the underlying cause are distinct. Lowering the set point improves fever while diagnostic reasoning continues.

questions.question: A patient receiving chronic systemic glucocorticoids has thin skin and delayed closure of a minor wound. Which mechanism best explains the impaired repair?
choices: Suppressed inflammatory signaling and fibroblast/collagen activity weaken coordinated healing
Enhanced macrophage activation and excessive early collagen cross-linking
Increased angiogenesis and epithelial proliferation accelerate closure
Selective stimulation of skeletal-muscle hyperplasia diverts neutrophils
rationales: Glucocorticoids can blunt inflammatory cell function and inhibit fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis.
The expected effect is suppression rather than enhanced macrophage and collagen activity.
Glucocorticoids can impair rather than accelerate these repair processes.
Skeletal-muscle hyperplasia is unrelated to the wound findings.
questions.explanation: Successful repair requires enough inflammation to control contamination and initiate later phases; excessive suppression can delay healing.

questions.question: A patient with chronic viral hepatitis develops progressive fibrosis despite fluctuating aminotransferases. Which process most directly drives the structural change?
choices: Persistent injury and cytokine signaling activate matrix-producing cells, causing excess extracellular matrix deposition
Repeated acute swelling permanently regenerates normal architecture without scarring
Neutrophils convert directly into hepatocytes
Apoptotic bodies synthesize collagen after phagocytosis
rationales: Chronic injury can sustain profibrotic signaling and activate fibroblast-like matrix-producing cells, progressively distorting tissue architecture.
Persistent injury can outpace regeneration and lead to scarring rather than guaranteed restoration.
Neutrophils do not transdifferentiate into hepatocytes in this process.
Collagen is produced by activated mesenchymal cells, not apoptotic fragments.
questions.explanation: Fibrosis is an excessive or persistent repair response. Injury-marker fluctuations do not necessarily mirror cumulative architectural damage.
